cards.title: Structure emails for clicks and replies, not just opens
cards.summary: Adopt conventions that maximize the metrics inbox providers weigh most: clicks, replies and engagement diversity.
cards.use_when: Writing or redesigning campaign templates after a low click-through or low reply rate.

cards.title: Use AI to analyze exported campaign analytics
cards.summary: Export Klaviyo campaign data and prompt an AI to surface bottlenecks and prioritized tests.
cards.use_when: You lack analyst bandwidth and need a quick diagnostic of recent campaign performance.

cards.title: Use AI to diagnose flow performance and prioritize tests
cards.summary: Export Klaviyo flow analytics, analyze with AI, then focus testing on the flows and emails carrying the most revenue.
cards.use_when: Deciding which email flow to optimize next, or auditing a mature automation program.

cards.title: Where welcome-flow revenue actually concentrates
cards.summary: Expect the first email of a welcome series to carry most revenue and rethink the purpose of later emails.
cards.use_when: Auditing or rebuilding a welcome/onboarding flow.

cards.title: Spot under-monetized flows and channel gaps
cards.summary: Use flow analytics to find flows with high opens but weak clicks or orders, and consider SMS as a follow-up for non-clickers.
cards.use_when: Reviewing browse abandonment, cart abandonment and cross-channel follow-up performance.

cards.title: 2026 deliverability KPI targets for ecommerce email
cards.summary: Set measurement thresholds for open, click, spam-complaint and unsubscribe rates before diagnosing strategy.
cards.use_when: Reviewing Klaviyo campaign health or setting reporting thresholds for an email program.

cards.title: Sequence the email system as a connected chain, not isolated tactics
cards.summary: Build ecommerce email in a dependency order where signup feeds flows, flows capture intent, campaigns create momentum, tests sharpen winners and deliverability keeps it all reaching the inbox.
cards.use_when: When planning the next quarter of email work or deciding which email project to start next in an ecommerce store.

cards.title: Audit your email program against the six-layer dependency model
cards.summary: Use a six-layer checklist (signup, flows, campaigns, testing, segmentation, deliverability) to find the weakest link limiting email revenue.
cards.use_when: When email revenue has plateaued and you need to diagnose which stage of the ecommerce email program to invest in next.

cards.title: Write 12 months of emails in one sitting
cards.summary: Block out a full year of emails in a single session so the perceived cost of starting an email program collapses.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to start or restart a store email program and dreading the ongoing workload.

cards.title: Plain-text email format to stay out of the Promotions tab
cards.summary: Format marketing emails to look like a personal note — text-heavy, no images, one or two links — so filters treat them as real correspondence.
cards.use_when: Planning the HTML/template for any store campaign email, especially retention and re-engagement sends.

cards.title: The Money Minute structure: reward on every step
cards.summary: Use a fixed four-part email skeleton that rewards the reader for opening, for reading, and for clicking.
cards.use_when: Designing the standard template for a recurring store newsletter or retention email.

cards.title: Reward every step with a feedback-loop email design
cards.summary: Behavior repeats when it was rewarded last time, so design each email so opening, reading and clicking each deliver a payoff.
cards.use_when: Restructuring an underperforming store newsletter or welcome sequence where readers open but never act.

cards.title: Reply Yes onboarding to train provider reputation
cards.summary: Require new subscribers to reply 'Yes' to receive the lead magnet, so engagement signals raise sender reputation.
cards.use_when: Setting up or revising the welcome and lead-magnet delivery flow for a store's opt-in.

cards.title: Make unsubscribing easy to protect deliverability
cards.summary: Reduce friction on unsubscribes because dormant subscribers hurt domain reputation more than people who leave cleanly.
cards.use_when: Configuring the unsubscribe link, preference center and list hygiene for a store's email program.

cards.title: Segment the list by qualifier answers at opt-in
cards.summary: Collect qualifiers like revenue band or business stage at signup and send content matched to the segment.
cards.use_when: Designing the opt-in form and deciding who receives which store campaign or educational email.

cards.title: Make CTR the primary email metric, not open rate
cards.summary: Track clicked actions over opens because Apple privacy changes make open data unreliable and CTR is what predicts revenue.
cards.use_when: Choosing the KPI for a store email program and reviewing send-to-send performance.

cards.title: Split-test subject lines on a slice, then send the winner
cards.summary: Test subject lines (and preview text) on a small portion of the list, then blast the winning variant to the rest.
cards.use_when: Optimizing subject-line performance for recurring brand emails or product campaigns.

cards.title: Send at the right day and hour for B2C vs B2B
cards.summary: Match send day and time window to audience type, since consumer and business inboxes peak differently.
cards.use_when: Scheduling a store's campaign or newsletter sends across a week.

cards.title: Keep cadence high but content value-only
cards.summary: Send roughly three times a week if every send is genuinely valuable, and fold the CTA into the value rather than running separate promo emails.
cards.use_when: Setting the sending frequency and give/ask balance for a store's list.

cards.title: Optimize for mobile rendering before sending
cards.summary: Check how every email renders on mobile, since most recipients will read it there and poor rendering kills clicks.
cards.use_when: Final QA before sending any store email, especially image- or layout-heavy templates.

cards.title: Confine links and CTAs to one per objective
cards.summary: Use one or two links per email, each tied to a distinct audience or objective, instead of sprinkling many links.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many links and buttons a store email should contain.

cards.title: Use annual renewal fees to lift revenue without touching the headline price
cards.summary: Add a one-time annual fee on top of a monthly subscription, charged after the first year, to increase revenue without hurting front-end conversion.
cards.use_when: Pricing a subscription, membership or replenishment program in a store.

cards.title: Turn testimonials into hooks by asking for the worst moment
cards.summary: Collect testimonial answers as a specific worst-moment story rather than a before/after narrative, so the quote works as an ad hook.
cards.use_when: Sourcing customer testimonials for a store's PDP, ads or email content.

cards.title: Give away a peeled-off bonus to make list membership worth something
cards.summary: Create exclusive assets that only list subscribers receive, so opt-in is sold on ongoing membership rather than the lead magnet alone.
cards.use_when: Designing the incentive stack for a store's email opt-in.

cards.title: Prioritize fast follow-up over almost everything else
cards.summary: Respond to an opt-in within seconds — the source says it could quadruple sales and argues it should be the first operational priority.
cards.use_when: Deciding what to fix first in a store's lead handling and conversion process.

cards.title: Focus effort on CTR over open rate over time
cards.summary: Optimize the rolling click-through rate rather than individual sends, treating high-value hard asks as withdrawals against softer sends.
cards.use_when: Planning a store's monthly email mix and reviewing whether the program is trending up or down.

cards.title: Use native-style links for deliverability
cards.summary: Route clicks to links that inbox providers already recognize as legitimate rather than to raw hosted sales pages.
cards.use_when: Choosing where a store's email link should point — sales page, video or gated document.

cards.title: Pre-flight: run audience + objection research before drafting any email copy
cards.summary: Run a few hours of structured research on competitor ads, Amazon reviews, podcasts and social profiles to build a research doc you write emails from.
cards.use_when: You are about to write a campaign, welcome flow or promo email and don't yet have written pain points, angles and objections for the product.

cards.title: Mine Amazon reviews for pre-purchase objections, not praise
cards.summary: Read most-recent Amazon reviews of competing and adjacent products to collect the specific objections (taste, difficulty of use, lead content, purification) you'll neutralise in copy.
cards.use_when: You are building objection-handling copy, review blocks or a guarantee for a consumable or problem-solution product.

cards.title: Pressure-test the market by searching Facebook Ad Library for problem keywords
cards.summary: Search Ad Library for the underlying problem (e.g. hair loss) rather than your product name to see what solutions already exist and what people complain about.
cards.use_when: You are deciding which angle or mechanism to lead with in acquisition emails or cold traffic and want evidence your framing is unsolved elsewhere.

cards.title: Extrapolate benefits into underlying insecurities to write empathetic copy
cards.summary: Map each surface product benefit down to the specific insecurity it compensates for, then write to the insecurity rather than the feature.
cards.use_when: You are writing longer-form benefit highlight copy or story blocks and the current draft reads generic or feature-led.

cards.title: Shift the blame outward to remove shame from the buying decision
cards.summary: Redirect responsibility for the customer's problem onto external factors so the reader is the victim rather than the cause, lowering the emotional cost of buying.
cards.use_when: You are writing problem-solution copy for a category where the customer may feel personally responsible for their problem (damaged hair, low energy, poor skin, low testosterone).

cards.title: Build emails from modular blocks instead of writing long-form direct response
cards.summary: Treat every ecommerce email as an assembly of standard blocks (banner, CTA, review, product display, benefit highlight, content/story, countdown, featured-on, guarantee) and write copy per block.
cards.use_when: You are briefing a designer, creating Klaviyo templates, or training a junior writer on how to produce campaign and flow emails quickly.

cards.title: Write the banner block to state the email's purpose above the fold
cards.summary: The banner is everything visible on a phone without scrolling, so its job is to state the email's offer or intent in one eye-catching hit.
cards.use_when: You are drafting the top of a promotional, launch or flow email and want to maximise scroll-through to the rest of the message.

cards.title: Keep CTA button copy to a single clear instruction
cards.summary: Button text only needs to tell the reader where to click and what happens next — the source says this is not hard to write and shouldn't be overthought.
cards.use_when: You are filling in button labels across a campaign, flow or template in your ESP.

cards.title: Select review blocks that answer a specific known objection
cards.summary: Replace generic 'I love it' testimonials with reviews that directly neutralise a pre-purchase anxiety you identified in research.
cards.use_when: You are populating the social-proof block of an email or flow and want it to move undecided readers rather than decorate the email.

cards.title: Choose the product display layout before writing the copy
cards.summary: Decide between row-by-row and grid formats based on how much copy each product needs and how it will render on a phone.
cards.use_when: You are laying out a merchandising email that features one hero product or several SKUs.

cards.title: Choose icon rows or longer copy for benefit highlights
cards.summary: Icon rows let you show several benefits at once; longer copy lets you tackle one benefit and its underlying insecurity in depth.
cards.use_when: You are writing the benefits section of an email and deciding how much persuasive copy to attach to each claim.

cards.title: Use fact-only content and story blocks when you don't know copywriting tactics
cards.summary: For founders writing their own emails, content blocks can simply present a study or a factual founding story — no framework required — and still sell.
cards.use_when: You are a small brand owner writing an education, brand-story or ingredient email without a copywriter or an established voice-of-customer library.

cards.title: Use countdown timers to back an urgency claim
cards.summary: A countdown timer only works as urgency if it is tied to a real, expiring claim such as a 24-hour discount code.
cards.use_when: You are running a launch or sale email where an offer genuinely expires and you want urgency without writing more persuasive copy.

cards.title: Feature logos as an authority block using 'as seen on' wording
cards.summary: The featured-on block is a simple trust signal: two wordings and a row of publication or show logos.
cards.use_when: You are adding a credibility layer to a welcome, launch or promotion email and have genuine press or media appearances to show.

cards.title: Reverse risk with a long unconditional guarantee — and expect fewer returns
cards.summary: Offer a long guarantee window on consumables to remove the fear of loss; the source argues a 180-day window will return less than a 30-day window in practice.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to add a guarantee block to acquisition or first-purchase emails and how long the window should be.

cards.title: Profile followers and ad comments to pin down who actually buys
cards.summary: Scan a competitor's Instagram followers and comment sections to infer the real demographics, age ranges and interests of the buying audience.
cards.use_when: You need a sharper customer profile for email segmentation, creative angles or list targeting and analytics only gives you aggregate age and gender.

cards.title: Test SMS/email send frequency with a holdout to prove incrementality
cards.summary: Design a cohort split (normal / zero / double) to measure whether extra messages actually lift revenue before scaling budget.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to increase lifecycle message cadence or justify a growing SMS bill to leadership.

cards.title: Set an SMS frequency baseline using subscriber LTV and unsub rate
cards.summary: Use subscriber LTV (acquisition rate, messages per subscriber, revenue per message, unsub rate) to find the send cadence that maximizes revenue without spiking unsubscribes.
cards.use_when: Setting or revising monthly SMS cadence and worried about annoying the list.

cards.title: Treat SMS as an acquisition channel, not just retention
cards.summary: Most people who give you a phone number haven't bought yet, so SMS flows are the welcome mat for paid traffic—manage and optimize them like performance marketing.
cards.use_when: Allocating team ownership, budget, or optimization effort across paid acquisition and lifecycle channels.

cards.title: Add a question to lifecycle flows to start conversations
cards.summary: The lowest-effort entry to conversational commerce is appending a simple question to an existing flow message and reading the replies.
cards.use_when: Starting conversational commerce or sourcing zero-party data without new tooling.

cards.title: Match conversation strategy to consideration period and ticket size
cards.summary: When and how aggressively to open conversations depends on how long buyers deliberate and how high the stakes are.
cards.use_when: Designing whether flows should lead with conversation or stay broadcast-first for a given product category.

cards.title: Use conversation data to build real zero-party customer attributes
cards.summary: Conversations surface static facts and ephemeral attributes you can operationalize across text and your CDP.
cards.use_when: Enriching subscriber profiles with personalization data and building one-to-one messaging.

cards.title: Use SMS/MMS/RCS as distinct channels and enable RCS for richer actions
cards.summary: RCS is a separate messaging channel with SMS fallback that raises the creative ceiling with carousels, video, and native action buttons.
cards.use_when: Planning SMS creative formats and considering RCS rollouts for launches or drops.

cards.title: Adapt to customer data through conversations
cards.summary: Persistent conversations uncover the objections preventing purchase that no PDP can pre-empt, so build a process to capture and act on those objections.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing mid-funnel purchase blockers and reducing friction at PDP and checkout.

cards.title: Chase incremental value in retention channels as paid channels saturate
cards.summary: As the curve of paid acquisition flattens, finer optimization of lifecycle messaging on owned channels becomes the marginal growth lever.
cards.use_when: Setting next-quarter growth priorities and allocating between paid acquisition and lifecycle optimization.

cards.title: Align pop-ups, flows, and campaigns to the true purchase decision
cards.summary: Pop-ups and welcome flows are acquisition touch points; campaigns are retention—design and own them accordingly.
cards.use_when: Deciding ownership and testing scope for pop-ups, welcome series, and campaigns.

cards.title: RCS vs SMS/MMS: what changes in the message
cards.summary: RCS is a distinct messaging protocol with SMS fallback that upgrades text-only or single-image messages into rich carousels, video, web views and native action buttons.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to pilot RCS for campaign sends or transactional/drop messaging, and scoping which message formats to build for it.

cards.title: Test RCS by holding out or running a clean flow
cards.summary: Operationalize an RCS switch with either a holdout group for incremental read or a deliberately simple one-to-one flow for a cleaner test signal.
cards.use_when: Launching or planning a first RCS campaign and needing to decide how to structure the test so results are trustworthy.

cards.title: Conversational carousels for product recommendation
cards.summary: Use RCS carousels inside a conversational thread to answer 'what do you recommend' with a small set of tailored best-sellers plus a native web view.
cards.use_when: Merchandising and PDP/landing-page substitution inside SMS/RCS: when a customer asks for a recommendation and you need to move them to a purchase path in-thread.

cards.title: List growth first: fix pop-up opt-in rate
cards.summary: For a $5–10M brand trying to grow SMS, the highest-leverage first move is on-site opt-in rate, because list size is the top of the funnel for every downstream send.
cards.use_when: Auditing SMS as an acquisition/growth channel and deciding where to spend first effort on list growth.

cards.title: Raise send cadence until unsubscribe rate ticks up
cards.summary: Increase message frequency one send at a time and let unsubscribe rate find your new ceiling, then treat that as the baseline.
cards.use_when: Setting campaign cadence for an established SMS program and deciding how many sends per week the list can absorb.

cards.title: Ask customers why they didn't buy to feed all flows
cards.summary: Run conversational questions to surface purchase objections, then push that learning into your team and every flow — not just to generate incremental revenue.
cards.use_when: Running conversational SMS and using customer-research output to improve abandoned-cart, win-back, PDP and objection-handling flows.

cards.title: Capture experiment learnings causally so the model earns trust
cards.summary: Operationalizing incrementality means running geo-lift and causal experiments and feeding them into your measurement model, so channel decisions are informed by tested lift rather than a black box.
cards.use_when: Attributing and budgeting across SMS/email/paid channels where you need to know which sends add incremental revenue versus cannibalize.

cards.title: Tactical SMS starting order for a mid-size brand
cards.summary: The source's recommended sequence for a $5–10M brand under-using SMS: fix pop-up opt-in, then expand cadence until unsubs rise, then add conversational questions.
cards.use_when: Prioritizing the first 30–90 days of an SMS improvement program when the team is lean and everything feels urgent.

cards.title: Checklist cadence: SMS/retention program for a growing brand
cards.summary: Small ecommerce teams run everything interconnected and hourly, so list health, cadence and message content should be managed as one operating rhythm.
cards.use_when: Running the day-to-day SMS/email lifecycle for a small ecom team and setting the review rhythm for list, cadence and messaging.

cards.title: Sizing the SMS channel for your store
cards.summary: SMS is an owned retention channel; source argues it should account for at least 5–15% of brand total sales and cites client SMS bills under $1,000/month producing tens of thousands monthly.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch or resource an SMS channel, or benchmarking whether your current SMS program is underperforming relative to the channel's potential.

cards.title: Choose and configure an SMS platform for Shopify-style ecommerce
cards.summary: Pick Klaviyo, Attentive or Postscript — they all do the same core job — and configure number verification, subscriber import, signup forms, opt-out language, smart sending, quiet hours and keyword responses.
cards.use_when: Setting up an SMS sending account for the first time, or migrating existing SMS subscribers into a platform that also holds your email.

cards.title: Two-step pop-up to convert email visitors into SMS subscribers
cards.summary: Split email and SMS into separate pop-up steps, lead with your best offer in the email step, and use 'finish signing up with text to activate 20% off' style copy on the SMS step.
cards.use_when: Building or redesigning an onsite pop-up whose goal is to grow an SMS list from traffic you are already paying for.

cards.title: Other SMS list-growth levers beyond the pop-up
cards.summary: The pop-up is the single biggest SMS list driver; the source frames seven growth methods and treats list growth as non-negotiable because an ungrown list caps campaign and flow reach.
cards.use_when: Planning next quarter's SMS subscriber acquisition when pop-up opt-ins alone are not adding enough subscribers.

cards.title: Write SMS campaigns that only say things worth interrupting for
cards.summary: SMS cannot afford to be vague: use clear, direct intents — sales, early access, restocks, back-in-stock, launches — because a 160-character message has no room for bland nurture content.
cards.use_when: Drafting the SMS slot in your campaign calendar, or reviewing a flat-performing SMS calendar that is heavy on general brand messaging.

cards.title: Set SMS sending frequency: one to two campaigns per week, never more
cards.summary: Keep SMS at about one campaign per week (two only for brands pushing over 8 figures annually), because frequency above that drives unsubscribes and annoyance faster than it adds revenue.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many SMS campaign sends per week to schedule, or diagnosing an unsubscribe rate climbing above 1%.

cards.title: Build a calendar from retail events, not nurture filler
cards.summary: Plan SMS around fixed retail moments — back-in-stock, seasonal launches, gifting holidays, big sale weekends, VIP early access, product spotlights and flash sales — with big events getting multiple sends.
cards.use_when: Laying out next month's SMS campaign calendar for a fashion or seasonal ecommerce brand.

cards.title: Schedule SMS outside quiet hours and coordinate email timing
cards.summary: Choose recipient-appropriate send times and test email/SMS spacing without treating a source time window as universal.
cards.use_when: Choosing send times for SMS campaigns and pairing them with the day's email send.

cards.title: Run SMS as a single-message omni-channel flow
cards.summary: Automated SMS flows are triggered by list signup, cart abandonment or product browse; most may legally contain only one SMS message (welcome is the exception with two), and they should run blended with email in one flow.
cards.use_when: Building the abandoned-cart, browse-abandonment and welcome automations for a store, or auditing whether existing SMS flows are compliant.

cards.title: Measure SMS on clicks, unsubscribes and delivery — not open rates
cards.summary: Open rate is a vanity metric for SMS; target a 5–15% click rate, keep unsubscribe below 1% (excellent below 0.5%) and delivery above 90–95%.
cards.use_when: Reporting on SMS campaign performance, or setting up the dashboard and review cadence for the SMS channel.

cards.title: Avoid wasting budget through non-compliance and message-length errors
cards.summary: SMS law is stricter than email: never send to anyone who has not explicitly opted in, keep most flows to one message, avoid MMS costs, stay inside quiet hours and watch the 160-character limit.
cards.use_when: Auditing SMS list segments and send rules before a campaign, or onboarding a new SMS platform to reduce avoidable spend and legal risk.

cards.title: Klaviyo (or similar ESP) account setup essentials for a new store
cards.summary: Order of operations for launching an email platform: connect store, choose opt-in mode, set up a branded sending domain and DMARC before sending anything.
cards.use_when: Launching or migrating the store's email lifecycle platform (Klaviyo or similar) and deciding which technical settings must exist before the first campaign or flow sends.

cards.title: Rate signup forms against a 2–4% baseline and target 8–12%
cards.summary: Typical ecommerce brands convert 2–4% of visitors into subscribers while optimized popups reach around 8–12%, so judge forms against the high-converting band.
cards.use_when: Benchmarking the store's email capture rate and deciding whether the popup needs a rebuild to hit list-growth targets.

cards.title: Build a high-converting popup: offer, headline, single field, big CTA
cards.summary: Popup anatomy that converts: an attractive offer stated in the headline, one email field, a large contrasting CTA, and a de-emphasized alternate option.
cards.use_when: Designing or redesigning the email capture popup for the storefront.

cards.title: Timing and display rules for capture popups
cards.summary: Display the popup after 4–10 seconds or 40–80% scroll (the source uses ~6s / ~60%) and treat the OR-vs-AND rule toggle as the main audience-size lever.
cards.use_when: Configuring when the store's popup appears so it captures engaged visitors without annoying first-timers.

cards.title: Always build separate mobile and desktop popups
cards.summary: One form for both devices fails: clone the desktop form into a mobile-only version and resize fields, buttons and teasers for touch.
cards.use_when: Finishing the capture popup build and preparing it for mobile traffic, which is most of an ecommerce store's visitors.

cards.title: Withhold the discount code from the success page
cards.summary: Show 'check your inbox' on the post-signup success page so the first welcome email earns the open and the code, protecting deliverability and inbox training.
cards.use_when: Designing the popup success page and the first welcome email after email capture.

cards.title: Teaser tab: keep the capture offer permanently reachable
cards.summary: A small persistent tab ('Save 10% now') lets visitors reopen the popup after closing it and adds a second capture surface.
cards.use_when: Adding a persistent capture element to the storefront after a visitor dismisses the popup.
